content: Pre-labor, also referred to as Prodromal Labor, represents the initial signs that occur before the onset of active labor. It is the body's natural process of preparing for true labor. Despite being commonly mischaracterized as false labor, prodromal labor shares similarities with traditional labor in its onset but does not progress to the delivery of the baby. Not all individuals are aware of this stage of labor, even though it occurs universally. However, this does not imply that every pregnant individual will experience all the associated symptoms. The term pre-labor is used to describe a collection of physical changes that may occur in a pregnant individual prior to the initiation of active labor. These changes can include an increase in blood volume, which may sometimes lead to swelling (edema), the occurrence of Braxton Hicks contractions, the presence of colostrum in the breasts, and the expulsion of the mucous plug that has sealed the cervix throughout the pregnancy. The term false labor is occasionally used to describe a series of Braxton Hicks contractions that are mistakenly interpreted as true labor.
